summary: A proposal for a remote job service protocol suited to TIPs, which have little processing power and cannot support the Data Transfer or File Transfer Protocols. It explores attaching card readers and printers to a TIP, using remote batch terminals, and Telnet-like formats. It updates RFC 189.

plainLanguage.summary: A small network box cannot run fancy protocols, so this note finds simple ways for it to send jobs to a big computer and get printouts back.

subtitle: Remote job service protocol for low-powered network terminals

tldr.problem: TIPs (Terminal Interface Processors) cannot run the full Data Transfer or File Transfer protocols, but users need to submit jobs to and retrieve results from powerful remote computers.
tldr.mechanism: NETRJT uses TELNET-like commands over an operator connection to control data transfer connections. The server initiates secondary connections to TIP devices (printer, punch, reader) and handles data formatting and record folding.
tldr.outcome: TIP users can submit batch jobs and retrieve printouts using simple device commands, with UCLA-CCN planning to implement this protocol.

today: RFC 283 updates RFC 189 and remains a historical record of how the early ARPANET adapted protocols for constrained devices. Though NETRJT itself is not widely deployed, its design principles influenced later work on terminal access protocols.

sections.title: TIP Remote Job Entry
sections.content:
RFC 283 presents NETRJT, a Remote Job Entry protocol designed specifically for Terminal Interface Processors (TIPs). TIPs have very limited processing power and cannot support the full Data Transfer Protocol (DTP) or File Transfer Protocol (FTP). Existing remote job entry protocols like CCN's NETRJS were designed for more capable hosts.

NETRJT follows the general NETRJS model of using TELNET over an operator connection paired with simple secondary connections for data transfer. It allows TIP users to submit card-reader input, retrieve printer output, and use a punch device.
sections.plainLanguage: Small network boxes cannot handle big fancy file transfer protocols. NETRJT lets them use simple TELNET commands to send jobs and get printouts like a regular remote job terminal.

sections.title: Commands and Device Control
sections.content:
NETRJT provides commands for opening and closing data streams, with the server taking responsibility for initiating the connections. Unlike NETRJS, the server can open a secondary connection to any TIP socket upon command from the operator. Commands set data transfer protocol options: BS (byte stream), TT (TIP-tape protocol), or full DTP. Record format options include TELNET (CR/LF delimited), ASA carriage control, the RECORDS format, or COMPRESSED.

Additional commands set maximum record length (default 120 for printer, 80 for punch and reader) and transmission code (ASCII or EBCDIC). This per-device configurability gives remote operators fine control over job submission and output retrieval.
sections.plainLanguage: The operator types simple commands like OPEN PRINTER or SET SIZE to control what format data comes in and how big each record is.

sections.title: Typical Usage
sections.content:
To retrieve output, a user opens a printer connection and selects a job (either the first one or by name). The server sends print-line images as they become available. Stream control commands like BACKSPACE, RESTART, CANCEL and DEFER let users manage output. The server retains output until explicitly accepted via CLOSE or automatically via continuous stream mode.

For input, users open a reader connection and send card images. The server spools them, and jobs are accepted either when a server-specific end-of-job marker is seen, a new job begins, or the user issues CLOSE ACCEPT. UCLA-CCN and UCSB agreed to implement this protocol, storing sequence numbers with files to enable reliable restarts.
sections.plainLanguage: To get output, you open a printer, the computer sends your printout, then you can backspace or cancel if needed. To send input, you open a reader and send cards.
